content:
“Should I Make the Jump?”

Since posting my guide to getting a job at a startup, I’ve had the chance to reconnect with dozens of people - old friends I haven't seen in years, younger Duke friends who are early in their career arc, friends of friends, and even former colleagues from MS / TZP.
We’ve grabbed coffee, gone for walks, and hopped on Zooms to talk about what’s next. 
Almost every conversation has ended with the same question:
- How do I know if making this jump is the right move for me?
- Can I actually handle the pay cut?
- The uncertainty?
- The lack of prestige compared to the banks and consulting firms?

Here’s what I’ve told almost everyone - and it comes from my time at MS, in VC, and at Unify:
I feel like our goal in life (not just work) should be to optimize for learnings as fast as possible.

- Before college, that meant trying every sport and subject.
- In college, it meant meeting people and exploring different majors.
- But after graduation? I feel like most people forget.

We get stuck chasing titles, promotions, and prestige. And for some, that’s enough. But if you’re asking whether to make the jump - then something in you knows definitively there’s more to explore out there.

We certainly don’t need any reminder given the news in recent weeks, but our time on earth is limited. To live the fullest life, it’s really our duty to optimize for learnings as fast as possible so that you can do what you were put on this earth to do. And it should be your goal to get there as fast as possible.

Whether that’s becoming a founder… or a banker… or a chef on the Amalfi Coast cooking seafood pasta (that third one’s me) - the goal is to figure it out, and go do it.

Don’t wait for the perfect moment. Optimize for learning - and let that guide the rest.

Writing (real writing, not AI slop) feels like a lost art lately.

Tools like Wispr Flow let you dictate everything - code, Slack messages, even LinkedIn posts. It’s fast, efficient... but sometimes at the cost of thoughtfulness.

Writing has always been my way to slow down and make sense of what I actually think. It helped me break into VC when I started a Substack (linked below). It helped me stand out in interviews (and even do sourcing in VC more effectively). It helped me build a brand that feels real - not manufactured. 

At Unify, I loved putting together content that wasn’t just AI filler - but actual thought pieces that helped people understand what we were building and why it mattered. Even today, writing continues to open doors and spark conversations I never expected.

It doesn’t always go viral. But it resonates.

In a world where everything looks and sounds the same, your voice is your edge.
So take your time and try it. Use your voice and make your story heard.

It might not get a million impressions - but it might get you your first customer, your dream job (I cold emailed Unify!), or a kind message from someone who really needed to hear it.

Unify is a system of action - fast, opinionated, built for BDRs to execute outbound at speed.
Clay is a system of data - powerful, hacky, built for GTMEs who want total control and reuse.

Almost every difference between the two flows from that tradeoff.

I touch on things like how these tools think about work, why they’ll never fully converge, and where each one quietly fails.

article.subtitle: Garrett Wolfe

article.description: A handful of months ago I felt compelled to write a post about CRMs and how important they are.So many founders have asked questions about which ones

content:
We were not prepared for the feedback that came from the launch of our v1 for Galaxy 👀 

Mitch, Leon and I had spoken to hundreds of devs when we launched our Alpha / MVP. Teams were dying to get into the product and give it a try. They had been waiting for a product thats like the Cursor for Data.

We were so excited as first time founders that we picked our favorite 100 individuals from our waitlist and just let them in.

The feedback was really reassuring, but after all - this was an early stage product.

- There were a number of issues with auth (we had some people like Andrew Arnold 🤫 in an infinite sign up loop lol)
- There were visual glitches and occasionally problems connecting your databases
- Deleting sources crashed the app
- and dozens more

People were super impressed with the UI / UX, the performance of the app, and of course our context-aware AI copilot, but we had let too many people into the alpha, and it was difficult to triage each issue and see through the noise. We of course had bug reporting processes, channels for our users, and more - but it wasnt enough, and it was very manual.

In launching our beta in the next few weeks, we’ve spent a considerable amount of time determining how we want to deliver support and onboarding to our customers. A lot of these discussions have pushed us towards leveraging n8n. Despite coming from Unify I had never explored n8n in depth because I had a ton of trouble getting started and the systems are relatively complex. I’m great with Clay and Zapier and such, but was scared to jump in because of the complexity / cold start problem. 

But yesterday I spent a ton of time learning and we now have a super exciting bug report automation in n8n that we’re pumped to roll out to automate customer issues in slack → classification → linear ticket creation with human approval and AI from end to end.

What are the most exciting N8N automations have you built and how did you get over the cold start problem?

Will share more on our CS journey and N8N next week :)

The things I've been most excited to build come from video games I played as a kid

Growing up, I was a total video game nerd. I’d speed through my homework on the bus just to hop on Xbox and dive into Minecraft, Battlefield, or other games with my friends.

We weren’t just playing - we were exploring: hunting glitches, unlocking easter eggs, laughing at bugs. It sounds silly, but those moments were surprisingly formative. They taught me to stay curious and look at problems from weird angles.

My mom (understandably) hated my strong inclination and excitement to sit in front of the TV for multiple hours on end and used to put limits on how much I could play. These games have instilled a lot of nostalgic moments in me. And notably, a lot of them have been easter egg related.

So when Mitchell Bregman, Leon Kozlowski and I started building Galaxy - a modern SQL workspace for devs and data engineers - I knew we had an opportunity to bake in the same feeling: 
curiosity, 
nostalgia, 
surprise.

These are our people. The kinds of folks who appreciate an unexpected throwback or a clever in-joke hidden in the product.

Since day one, I’ve been lobbying Mitch hard (annoying him daily) to sneak in silly, delightful easter eggs - the kind that make devs laugh out loud

We have so many in app experiences and easter eggs and are always trying to build in more but here’s just a few of my favorites

- 🎮 We vibe coded all time classic mini games into the app like Galaga, Flappy Space (our version of Flappy Bird), and more are coming soon 🤫 😎
- 🎨 We have custom themes and color palettes that are fun, weird, and give the app more character. We obviously have a Candyland theme ;) (iykyk)
- 🏆 We have fun animations that celebrate in-app milestones, secret features and accolades, and tons more.
- 🔊 I’m currently negotiating with Mitchell Bregman to get the THX sound effect to play when someone enables AI in Galaxy for the first time (Yes, this idea is copyrighted by us. Don’t even think about stealing it.)

Honestly? This has been one of the most joyful parts of building Galaxy.
In a world full of boring dashboards and cookie-cutter SaaS, we want to build something people love to use. Something that makes you smile after a long day.

If you’ve got a funny, nostalgic, or ridiculous idea for Galaxy - drop it in the comments or DM me. If we ship it, we’ll give you credit in the product and in the community.

Let’s make data fun again. 💫

content:
Our reply rate on cold emailing at Galaxy is abysmal.  
Less than 0.5%.

It's not surprising, developers hate being sold to. 

And I’m not a good copywriter (Skyler Mickunas spent months teaching me copywriting and I still have tons of work to do).

But here’s the thing: outbound might not convert devs, but the signals behind it are still insanely useful.

It’s fairly well known that you can’t cold email developers. Many developers / engineers don’t even use their email, let alone will be receptive enough to read a sales email and reply.
And it’s true - they prefer to self-serve, try things on their own, and only pay when they have to..
But for lots of founders I’ve spoken with, turning off email (and outbound) typically means they turn their attention to other channels and forget about outbound. I actually believe this is shortsighted and here’s why:

1. It’s not about sending emails. It’s about why youre sending emails.
-  As a GTM guy, there’s no lesson more important than really nailing down why you have the god-given right (lol bc sellers act entitled) to send a cold email to someone. If it’s a warm lead, you actually have a good reason to reach out. Understanding this why is **crucial**. These intent signals will lay the foundation for how you prioritize lead scoring, how you build a sales team more broadly, and much more. 

2. Email is extremely cheap and allows you to experiment
- Some paid ads on LinkedIn or otherwise can cost hundreds of dollars for a single meeting booked / lead. A starter google workspace maibox costs $7 PER MONTH and you can send virtually unlimited number of emails during that time period (though I recommend no more than 25 per day lol). You can update email copy on a moment’s notice (copy, positioning, language, titles, etc.) and send tens of thousands of emails per day across hundreds of email mailboxes. It’s a no brainer from a customer acquisition cost perspective (CAC). 
Some people might hate me for this, but in the worst case, email serves as an educational channel or form of brand awareness -_-

Outbound won’t scale your dev tool. But the signals you uncover - and the messaging you refine - will fuel everything else.
Agree, disagree? What do you think?

content:
A $250K GTM engineer is the cheapest hire on your team.

Last week a founder of a fast-growing AI company asked me what to pay a top 1% GTM engineer. I said $250K base, $50K variable, generous equity. He was stunned.

He was anchored on the wrong comparison. Most people price a GTM engineer against an SDR or a RevOps manager and conclude $300K all-in looks like 2x too much. That's pricing a system-builder like an IC.

You're not hiring someone to work a book of business. You're hiring the person who builds the machine that works it for everyone else.

Here's the math I walked him through. 

Deliberately conservative, close to what I actually see across the dozen or so GTM teams I work with right now. One GTM engineer builds the programmatic pipeline layer: signal-based sourcing, enrichment, the plays that keep running whether or not anyone logs in.

- $3M net-new qualified pipeline (plays the team wasn't running before)
- x 20% close rate = $600K net-new ARR
- vs ~$300K fully loaded = 2x in year one

Halve the assumptions and you're roughly break-even. The hire pays for itself before you get generous.

And 2x is the floor, because it only counts new pipeline. 

It ignores what they also do: make the reps you already have better. Same rep, more accounts, a few points higher close rate, because the context is already sitting there instead of being researched cold. One hour of prep instead of eight. 

That's a separate reason the number holds -- I don't even stack it on top.

The salary went up and the cost per outcome went down. Those aren't the same thing, and confusing them is what makes people call this market overpriced.

The expensive hire was never the $300K engineer who returns 2 to 3x. It was the $120K one who kept the old playbook running and quietly cost you the year.

Some key takeaways that have helped us show up more often in AI-generated answers:
- Use FAQ-style question-and-answer formatting
- Start with a direct, concise answer - ideal for featured snippets
- Use proper heading tags (<h1>, <h2>, etc.) to structure your content
- Lists, bullets, and tables help make info skimmable
- Go deep in communities like Reddit to surface real user queries
- Internal linking builds topical authority and helps SEO
- Fast-loading pages (think LCP/core web vitals) are table stakes

---> And maybe most importantly - AEO starts with solid SEO. If your site isn’t technically sound and optimized for search, you’re probably invisible to AI engines too.

Creating a Sales Enablement Playbook is one of the highest leverage things you can do for a sales team (and your broader org). It cuts ramp time, builds confidence, and improves conversion dramatically.

At Unify, I became the first true “power user” of our product. I joined before emailing even existed in the platform - and my day-to-day usage helped pave the roadmap. Because of that, I was also the person new hires turned to for:

- how to use Unify,
- how we differentiated,
- and where GTM was headed.

As the product grew, the time I spent onboarding people ballooned. So last fall, I built Unify’s first Sales Enablement Playbook - a resource I wanted every new hire to treat as their bible for getting up to speed.

Inside, I captured:
- the history of outbound + intent signals
- why deliverability matters
- what Unify is (and isn’t) a good fit for
- ICP & lifecycle fit
- our competitive set + differentiation
- customer success stories
- onboarding requirements
- pricing & objection handling

It quickly became an invaluable resource for the team. 
And here’s the takeaway I’d share: build yours early. Update it often. Make it a living doc that evolves with your product and GTM motion.

If you’re thinking about building one - or want to shortcut by borrowing from my experience - drop a comment or reach out. I've already been building the v1 for Galaxy!!! Always happy to help.
